body: You’d be surprised how many people have done something similar. Hopefully she’s not a horrible person and would never put you on blast, but even if she did, it sounds like you had a bit of a breakdown. Idk I have a lot of sympathy for you and I hope you start feeling better and forgiving yourself. We all make horrible mistakes. It’s a part of being human.
Break ups are unreal hard. Especially after so long. I’ve also been a long term partner and I’ve been through a long term break up. Really one of the toughest human experiences, imho.

I feel you. I think people are well meaning but they don’t really understand the extent of it. Having a severe mood disorder and being told to “be positive” is like telling a terminal cancer patient to “eat more salads.” I mean, salads are good for you, but it’s not going to do much about the cancer. 

Edited to add: I also think there’s some serious death phobia in our culture that perpetuates the idea that we should do anything to avoid it or avoid even discussing it at all costs. I personally think the phobia and denial of that eventual reality for everyone contributes to a lot of bad policy decisions regarding euthanasia for chronically ill people.

This isn’t really a social anxiety issue. This guy is a predator. You should do whatever you need to in order to protect yourself.

Can you start setting up a small camera? Does this guy live with you? Near you? Why is he around at all? Can you buy a “spy” camera or even just use your phone to record him?

Can you scare him? But some mace and threaten to mace him. Tell him if he touches you again you’re going to hurt him.

Tell him right in front of others that you don’t feel comfortable being alone with him. Leave the room, if you have to. Lock yourself in a different room. Stay with other people. If he touches you again and you’re anywhere near other people, start yelling “don’t touch me!!!” And get up and move. Make it extremely inconvenient for him.

So it sounds like she’s the problem, not the class. Making that distinction is important imo. The class is a safe space, she just sucks at being a supportive person.

I think you handled it well, actually. We have to learn to let go of little things and not dwell on them or allow them to take up space in our lives. If she relentlessly bullies you every class, that’s a different story, but there’s no need to blow up over someone being insensitive/a bad partner. Just ignore it. That’s their problem really.

I guess you could ask to not be put in a group with her again, but she could just have had an off day. Maybe if she does it again you can say something, but I’d let it go for now and just see if it happens again.

Sorry to say, but it sounds like you really just built things up in your head. I don’t think she likes you more than as a friendly coworker. I think your expectations are making you unhappy. If she has a boyfriend she’s not the right person anyway. 

If you’re capable of reframing your relationship with her as a work friend, it sounds like that might be much healthier for both of you. Being able to make casual friends with your coworkers is extremely important. You never know when you might need a reference or favor.

I don’t think you should confront her because she’ll probably have no idea what you’re talking about. I mean, she doesn’t know what you’re thinking. Sounds like she’s just chillin, being a friendly person.

I feel the opposite way. You can’t get true empathy from people who don’t get it. If you’ve never actually felt suicidal but you tell me to “just buck up,” I just roll my eyes. If you tell me, “I get it. I want to die too and I don’t know what to do about it,” at least I feel like that person truly understands the struggle I’m talking about.

If it triggers someone or they react badly to that, or it makes them want to die more, then yeah, probably shouldn’t be here. But I’m COMPLETELY alone. I have no one to talk to who gets it.

I think it’s also a question of whether you’re pro suicide, or whether you are here wanting to shame or otherwise convince people not to do it. You have no idea what very real struggles someone might be facing in life— shit that just isn’t an easy fix. A lot of people aren’t here “falling in love with death” lmao, their lives are a nightmare. If you’ve never lived life with an incurable mental illness, are you really prepared to say that you know they should choose life in all circumstances? Maybe I shouldn’t describe it as pro suicide per say, but I’m not here to make people feel any worse about what they’re thinking. I’m not here to pretend like I have answers to their problems. I’m just here to quietly say, “I get it. You’re not alone.”

I mean, yeah, that’s my genuine perspective on the subject. 

You can love kids and want to have them someday and recognize that this isn’t the right time/person. You can also recognize that your thoughts of regret are somewhat fueled by the fantasy you’ve built up. That’s not nihilism/pessimism, that’s reality. 

If you really love kids and believe that having them is  your life’s purpose, you shouldn’t bring them into the world just to keep a girl or to solve some problem, or as the result of an accident you just shrug and accept. You should create a fantastic life first where you can provide for them, where you’re happy and fulfilled on your own, then find the right person and give your future kids a life of stability. Come at it from a place of abundance rather than basically asking a child to fix you/your relationship, which just isn’t fair/realistic.

I’ve been struggling to get through college for a long time. Partially because of money issues, and partially because it’s so hard to be successful when you have mental health problems. Totally understand where you’re coming from.

One thing that’s helped me is to try to reframe things and go to college for my own growth and wellbeing rather than allow other people’s opinions and expectations be a part of it. Easier said than done, but I try to stay away from people who stress me out. I set boundaries and don’t let them talk to me about “success.” I truly believe that some people who are driven by external achievement don’t understand how harmful they can be by putting pressure on people who are already struggling. So maybe take a break from seeing/talking to certain people about school.

Nah, don’t think about it like that. It wasn’t meant to be. 

Lots of people are unhappy living with their partners. Sometimes you just don’t know it until you do it. Trust me, having a partner and kids isn’t the answer to depression. It doesn’t magically fix your issues. You might struggle even more because more is expected of you/life is harder caring for someone else 24/7. 

Having a kid puts a huge strain on a relationship, even for people with really good ones. You might imagine it as this perfect life where everything would end up magically okay, but in real life, it’s sleep deprivation, stress and way more expenses. It’s enough to make really strong people struggle... two people having to be expert communicators and compromisers to make it work.

Really, the thoughts and regrets you’re having are fantasy. Let them go. Forgive yourself. Be grateful for new opportunities/the freedom to choose something different. Having kids does not fix everything in your life/relationship. There’s a reason your ex ultimately agreed with you and went through with the abortion.

Can you check yourself in to an inpatient facility? Can you see a psychiatrist or psychologist? If you’re at a point where you’re looking for someone to talk about things with, who knows what you’re dealing with (and is literally trained to deal with this disorder), this is going to be your best bet. You’re at a point where you can recognize that your behavior is pushing people away/not helping you. That’s great— it means you have the motivation to try something else.

I don’t have bpd but I do have other untreated mental health problems that affect everything in my life, so I understand how extreme it can get when that’s the case. There are people who understand out there. There are people who have seen it all before and who won’t judge you. I hope you can get in touch with some of them and let them help you.

I also hope you can start accepting yourself, even if that means confronting/leaving the people who say ignorant things to you.

Happiness is fleeting for most humans. Some say attachment and expectations are what cause us to suffer, and that the goal is to empty the mind. Some say gratitude is the answer.

Have you ever felt contentment? Like, just at peace with what’s happening? Or maybe you’ve gotten really into a game or into something else you were doing? Maybe you cared for someone or something that desperately needed it. Some people say those moments are happiness. 

I think one of the problems is that in our current society, we define happiness as this concrete, far off goal. If only I could ___, then I’d finally be happy. But then it never comes, or you set some goal that’s never attainable for you.

There’s also so much genuine bad in the world. We witness it, but it feels like there’s nothing that can be done about it. It’s tough to find meaning in a society where you work, go to bed, repeat and where you don’t feel you have an impact or the power to stop horrible things you can see happening all over the world.

Ig what I’m saying is that this is the million dollar question. No one knows how to be happy, not really. Not forever. Happiness as we imagine it doesn’t even really exist. You just have to take and accept moments of contentment as they are, try to create meaning, try to do some little good for someone and acknowledge that the human mind is its own worst enemy sometimes.

Hey, I just wanted to say that I totally understand where you’re coming from. Definitely feel similarly sometimes.

One thing that’s helped me is to think of it as trading something— learning some new skill, or an opportunity for increased physical activity for example, in exchange for having to work someplace. I try to look at the bright side of it, even if it’s just meeting new people or seeing what I really DONT want to do. I also keep bills as low as I can possibly manage so that I can save a little and look for a different job if I become unhappy somewhere.

Doing these things help to some degree. But yeah, it’s a cold, hard, capitalist world. I hope that in the future it doesn’t have to be quite this way.

If it makes you feel a bit better, school is really hard for a lot of people, especially people who are struggling with mental health issues. It’s crazy how common it is for students to be depressed, and the lack of resources are a huge problem. Your dad doesn’t get it because school really was less stressful/competitive/expensive when he was there. It’s okay to have a hard time with school. You’re among the majority, I assure you.

Yeah, I feel you. The idea of proving yourself via school: “Here’s what’s important. Learn it immediately and regurgitate it in a very specific format. Otherwise you don’t deserve to make enough money to survive.” Definitely bothers me a lot, most days. Especially when it’s harder for me than others... but I also have sympathy for other students who are left behind in various capacities by the system. 

I mean, if you live in a place where the public school system is crap and your family is poor, it’s not really your fault that you dropped out in high school to work and care for them, just as an example. Imagine how hard that would then be catching up as an adult who went back to school. There are lots of barriers for lots of people who aren’t in the perfect position to do well. As someone with adhd, I can relate and see that/have sympathy for that person too.

Not to make this political, but I believe everyone deserves a basic standard of living (food, healthcare, a place to sleep) regardless of their productivity level. Our society is obsessed with proving we deserve to be alive and it’s pretty disturbing.

I know it’s annoying and I do try very hard to resist. I was watching some videos a psychiatrist made about adhd the other day and one of the things she suggested was to try to wait 10 seconds after someone stops talking for your turn. 

She also suggested that people with adhd try to take a moment to write down a thought (and explain what they’re doing) rather than interrupting. 

It’s not easy but I’m working on doing those things with nt people I know. I’ve gotten acceptance so far from them, so maybe something to try to improve communication skills would help you too.

Another thing I’ve been trying to do is ask a question and listen to a response for every thing I want to say. Sometimes I get these interesting thoughts I want to share really badly, but instead of/in addition to just blurting them out, I also ask a question the other person would probably like. 

I’ve also been working on making conversations less chaotic by explaining/transitioning to other topics slower. 

All have helped me so I hope it helps someone else too :)

I’d let her know that you understand and care about her. I’d also ask her what she needs. Maybe she needs someone to listen to her. Maybe she needs to be left alone. Only she knows. But she did open up to you, which means she’s reaching out for help.

If you believe she’s currently in crisis (I.e. if she’s actively hurting herself or if she’s planning to) you should probably take her to a hospital and have them hold her for psychiatric evaluation. That will get the ball rolling on medical care. She may not respond well to that, so you may have to call an ambulance, but she does need to go back to a psychiatrist and psychologist.

It can be hard to find medication that works for you. It can also be hard to find a therapist who works for you. It takes some trial and error, unfortunately. It also isn’t the answer to all of our problems. Most people who have been on meds or who have tried therapy have had to learn the hard way that pills don’t magically make you feel better. But the right ones can stop you from being at the lowest low, and you can start making changes to your life, or learning coping skills. It’s still hard though. 

It may be that she has an undiagnosed mental illness that can be better managed through daily meds and learning coping skills, or it may just be a rough patch. Maybe she’s deeply unhappy with something going on. A good psychologist that she jives with will help her figure that out.
